title: Dimensionality Reduction — PCA
summary: PCA end to end — the most-asked unsupervised technique in ML interviews, from variance intuition to the eigen-math and its real limitations.

slides.markdown:
**Principal Component Analysis (PCA)** compresses many correlated features into a handful of new, uncorrelated ones that capture most of the original variation.

Think of a photo of a pancake taken from directly above versus from the side — the side view (one flat dimension) loses almost nothing about its shape, because the pancake barely varies in height. PCA finds that best "flattest" viewing angle automatically, for data with hundreds of dimensions instead of three.

slides.subTitle: The curse of dimensionality
slides.markdown:
As you add features, data gets **sparser** in the resulting space — points that seemed close in 2D end up almost equally far apart in 200D, which breaks distance-based methods like KNN and clustering, and makes models more prone to overfitting on noise.

This is the **curse of dimensionality**. Reducing to fewer, information-dense dimensions fights it directly: less noise, faster training, and distances that mean something again.

slides.subTitle: Directions of maximum variance
slides.markdown:
PCA looks for the direction in the data along which points spread out the **most** — that's the **first principal component**. Then it finds the next-best direction that's perpendicular to the first, and so on.

Why variance? Because the direction with the most spread is the direction carrying the most information — a direction where all points look nearly identical tells you almost nothing about which point is which. Keeping only the top few components keeps most of that information while dropping dozens of dimensions.

slides.subTitle: Seeing the components
slides.markdown:
On a 2D scatter, PCA's first component is the line the data is most stretched along; the second is perpendicular to it.

![Principal components over a 2D scatter](assets/pca-components.svg)

Projecting every point onto just PC1 keeps most of the spread — you'd lose remarkably little by dropping PC2 entirely, which is exactly the trade PCA makes at scale with many more dimensions.

slides.subTitle: Eigenvectors and eigenvalues
slides.markdown:
Mechanically, PCA computes the data's **covariance matrix** (how every feature varies with every other), then finds its **eigenvectors** and **eigenvalues**.

Each eigenvector is a principal component — a direction in feature space. Its paired eigenvalue is how much variance lies along that direction. Sorting eigenvectors by eigenvalue, largest first, gives you the ranked list of principal components — keep the top few, drop the rest.

slides.subTitle: Explained-variance ratio and the scree plot
slides.markdown:
Each component's **explained-variance ratio** is its eigenvalue divided by the sum of all eigenvalues — the share of total variance it captures.

A **scree plot** graphs these ratios in order; you typically keep enough components to cross a target cumulative variance (often 90–95%), or stop where the plot's curve flattens out. There's no universally "correct" number — it's a trade-off between compression and information kept.

slides.subTitle: Skipping standardization
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "PCA works fine on raw features regardless of their scale."

**Why it's wrong:** PCA chases the directions of highest **variance**, and variance is scale-dependent. A feature measured in thousands (like income) will dominate one measured in single digits (like age) purely because of units, not because it's actually more informative.

**Correct model:** always **standardize** features (zero mean, unit variance) before running PCA, unless every feature is already on a genuinely comparable scale.

slides.subTitle: What you lose
slides.markdown:
Principal components are **linear combinations** of the original features — "0.6×income − 0.3×age + 0.2×tenure" — not a single original feature you can name and explain to a stakeholder.

That's the real cost of PCA: you trade interpretability for compression. It's a fine trade when the downstream job is prediction or visualization, but a poor one when a business team needs to know *which original feature* is driving an outcome.

slides.subTitle: When straight-line variance isn't the right lens
slides.markdown:
PCA only ever looks for **straight-line** directions of maximum variance — it fundamentally cannot capture curved structure. Data shaped like a spiral or an S-curve in high dimensions has an obvious low-dimensional structure, but PCA's linear projections will slice through it in a way that destroys that structure rather than preserving it, because no straight line captures a curve's shape.

This is exactly the gap that nonlinear methods like t-SNE and UMAP (see [Dimensionality Reduction — t-SNE & UMAP](dimensionality-reduction-tsne-umap)) exist to fill — they preserve local neighborhood structure regardless of whether it's linear, at the cost of the clean, reversible, variance-ranked components PCA provides.
